Start before history taking

•Evert lids, remove particulate matter
•Check pH until neutral
•Debride necrotic epithelium (by ophthalmologist)

Assessment & Management
•ABC of trauma
•Protect eye with rigid shield (never patch / press)
•Never measure IOP
•Record visual acuity
•Nil per os (NPO) → for general anesthesia
•IV antibiotics
•Immediate ophthalmology referral
Investigations
•CT scan (best for IOFB localization)
•MRI contraindicated if metallic FB suspected
•Plain X-ray for radiopaque FBs

stem: All of the following tests are useful in evaluating a patient with a retained iron intraocular foreign body EXCEPT:
All of the following tests are useful in evaluating a patient with a retained iron intraocular foreign body EXCEPT:
explanation_verbatim: MRI is contraindicated in patients with possible iron intraocular foreign bodies because magnetic forces may move the metal, causing further eye injury. CT scan and ultrasound are safe alternatives.

stem: Which is the most dangerous and has bad prognosis?
Which is the most dangerous and has bad prognosis?
explanation_verbatim: Alkali burns penetrate ocular tissues rapidly, causing severe and deep damage to the cornea and anterior segment. Acid burns tend to coagulate proteins and thus are less penetrating.

options: Total hyphema with prolonged rise in IOP

stem: Corneal blood staining is due to:
options: Total hyphema with prolonged rise in IOP
explanation_verbatim: Corneal blood staining occurs when total hyphema is accompanied by persistently high intraocular pressure, forcing red cells and hemoglobin into the cornea.

stem: A 25-year-old male patient presented with left enophthalmos. He gave history of receiving a punch in that eye 6 months ago. On examination, there was hypoesthesia over the left side of the nose, upper lip, upper teeth, and gum. Which of the following nerves is commonly affected?

A 25-year-old male patient presented with left enophthalmos. He gave history of receiving a punch in that eye 6 months ago. On examination, there was hypoesthesia over the left side of the nose, upper lip, upper teeth, and gum. Which of the following nerves is commonly affected?
explanation_verbatim: A blow-out fracture of the orbital floor damages the infraorbital nerve, leading to numbness over the cheek, upper lip, and gums. Enophthalmos and restricted eye movement may also occur.

stem: A 35-year-old blacksmith presents after being struck in the eye by a piece of iron while working. On examination, his intraocular pressure is decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to perform?

A 35-year-old blacksmith presents after being struck in the eye by a piece of iron while working. On examination, his intraocular pressure is decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to perform?
explanation_verbatim: CT scan of the orbit is the best investigation for metallic intraocular foreign bodies, as MRI is contraindicated in such cases. It helps assess the location and depth of the foreign object.

stem: A man presents after ocular trauma with decreased vision in one eye. He was previously emmetropic, but now has a refractive error of +10 diopters in the affected eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A man presents after ocular trauma with decreased vision in one eye. He was previously emmetropic, but now has a refractive error of +10 diopters in the affected eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Loss of the natural lens (aphakia) causes a high hypermetropic shift (+10D). This often occurs after lens dislocation or surgical removal.

stem: A patient presents after ocular trauma, and ophthalmoscopic examination reveals a white crescent-shaped streak at the posterior pole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A patient presents after ocular trauma, and ophthalmoscopic examination reveals a white crescent-shaped streak at the posterior pole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: A choroidal rupture appears as a crescent-shaped white streak at the posterior pole after blunt trauma due to tearing of Bruch’s membrane and the choroid.

stem: Definitive treatment of intraocular foreign body?
Definitive treatment of intraocular foreign body?
explanation_verbatim: Definitive treatment for an intraocular foreign body is prompt surgical removal to prevent complications such as endophthalmitis or siderosis bulbi.

stem: Which of the following represents imprinting of the iris lens on the anterior capsule of the lens from the pupillary margin?
Which of the following represents imprinting of the iris lens on the anterior capsule of the lens from the pupillary margin?
explanation_verbatim:
Vossious ring refers to imprinting of iris pigment on the anterior capsule of the lens from the pupillary margin (in case of blunt eye trauma).
Hypopyon → Pus in the AC (usually in neglected open wounds of the globe with secondary infection) [post-traumatic infectious endophthalmitis].
Hyphema → Haemorrhage in the anterior chamber. The source of bleeding is the iris root.

stem: What is the definitive management of a case presenting with an intra-ocular foreign body?
What is the definitive management of a case presenting with an intra-ocular foreign body?
explanation_verbatim: The initial management of a case presenting with an intra-ocular foreign body is copious irrigation. However, the definitive management of that case is surgical removal of the foreign body.

stem: Your neighbor, a 43-year-old woman, is cleaning her swimming pool. While she is pouring some concentrated algaecide into the pool, a large amount of this solution splashes into her right eye. When you hear her screams, you come to her aid less than 30 seconds after the injury. Which of the following should you do first?
options: Bundle her into your car and speed off for the nearest emergency center.
Run back to your study to look up the specific antidote for algaecide.
Carefully examine her eye for evidence of ocular hyperemia.
Copious irrigation with water from the nearest source instructing her to hold her eyes open to flush out chemical.
explanation_verbatim: Immediate and prolonged irrigation is the first and most critical step in any chemical eye injury. It reduces the contact time of the chemical with ocular tissues and prevents further damage.

stem: 25-year-old man complaining of decreased vision and pain in his right eye after being involved in a fist fight. There are edema and ecchymosis of the eyelids. His visual acuity is OD 6/12 and OS 6/6, pupils are round and reactive, normal IOP and no restriction of ocular motility. On examination of the anterior segment, you notice a diffuse haze in the anterior chamber and early layering of blood inferiorly. Regarding your diagnosis; Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?
options: Bed rest in 45 degree and close follow up with an ophthalmologist.
Prescribe steroid drops and antiglaucoma drops, and tell the patient to keep his head elevated.
Hospitalization and immediately call for an ophthalmologist.
Refer to ophthalmologist for surgical evacuation as soon as possible.

28-year-old male patient has pain, tearing and blurred vision in his right eye. Earlier in afternoon, while he had been working on his car with a hammer and chisel, he noticed that something flying into his right eye. Examination revealed that visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye. There is conjunctival hyperemia, the pupil seems to be peaked and pointing to the 7 o’clock position of the limbus. There is a small, dark, slightly elevated body at the 7 o’clock position of the limbus. The left eye is normal.
Which of the following would be the appropriate initial management for this situation?
options: Irrigation of the limbal foreign body
Removal of the limbal foreign body using a cotton-tipped applicator
Removal of the limbal foreign body using forceps

stem: 28-year-old male patient has pain, tearing and blurred vision in his right eye. Earlier in afternoon, while he had been working on his car with a hammer and chisel, he noticed that something flying into his right eye. Examination revealed that visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye. There is conjunctival hyperemia, the pupil seems to be peaked and pointing to the 7 o’clock position of the limbus. There is a small, dark, slightly elevated body at the 7 o’clock position of the limbus. The left eye is normal. Which of the following would be the appropriate initial management for this situation?
options: Irrigation of the limbal foreign body
Removal of the limbal foreign body using a cotton-tipped applicator
Removal of the limbal foreign body using forceps
explanation_verbatim: The peaked pupil and dark body at the limbus suggest a penetrating injury with intraocular foreign body. The eye should not be manipulated—apply a shield and refer urgently.
